# Synthesis — reading standard, 10 clips

## The non-negotiables (every clip, no exceptions)

**Caption-to-speech sync is frame-tight.** This is the one thing that never varies in quality across all ten, regardless of how different their styles are. Word-build timing lands exactly on the syllable it represents — not early, not trailing. If a caption placement is even a frame off, it reads as amateur against this bar. This is the first thing to check on any placement.

**Emphasis is always visually distinct from connective tissue.** Every single clip marks "the word that matters" differently from "the word that's just grammar" — bigger, bolder, colored, italicized, held longer. Plain undifferentiated caption text never appears anywhere in the set. But — important disagreement — *how* they mark it is never the same twice: clip 1 uses scale on numbers, clip 2 uses orange/blue color-coding, clip 6/9 (same account) use italic-for-connective/bold-caps-for-emphasis, clip 10 splits into two whole typographic registers. **There is no universal color or weight code. The rule is "differentiate," not "differentiate this way."** Pick a scheme per project and hold it consistently — don't reach for one clip's specific code as if it were the standard.

**Cuts land on caption completion, not arbitrarily.** Across the set, a cut very often happens in the exact frame a caption finishes building. Treat "does the caption finish right as the shot changes" as a real check, not a coincidence to ignore.

**Brand/product name gets its own clean beat, at least once.** Every promotional clip (1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10) gives the tool/brand name a standalone moment — full-screen icon, isolated word, or held caption — not buried mid-sentence at the same weight as everything else. It happens more than once when the video is long enough (mid-video reveal + CTA reveal).

**Software demos are real, never simulated.** Every clip that shows a product does it via genuine screen-recording with a visible cursor or finger actually performing the action, and a callout (color pill, drawn circle, spotlight vignette — device varies) points at the exact control the narration is naming *at that moment*. Never assume the viewer can find the referenced element unaided.

**Numbers and superlative claims always outweight their surroundings.** Dollar figures, percentages, "100," "60 days," "$2,000,000" — always bigger, bolder, or a different color than the sentence around them. This is universal even though the specific execution (odometer build vs. instant slam vs. oversized static) is not.

**The hook fires in the first ~3 seconds and builds toward a payoff word.** Every clip escalates its opening line word-by-word or phrase-by-phrase toward a punch (a dollar figure, "EDIT," "TRASH," "captions are stealing your time") rather than dropping the full sentence in at once. Broader premise-setting or tutorial content comes after this, never before it.

**B-roll always carries the caption thread through it.** Cutaways to hands typing, walking shots, product photography — captions never pause or go silent over a cutaway. The caption is the throughline; the visual is free to change underneath it.

## Where they genuinely disagree — do not treat the majority as a rule

**Endings are not standardized.** 7 of 10 (clips 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10) end on the same dark-navy TikTok-logo/gradient-bar/handle-searchbar template, multiplying into 3–5 copies. But clip 1 ends on a slow manual fade-to-black with the CTA caption frozen on top. Clip 2 ends on a static branded logo card, then a separate IG-watermark slate. Clip 10 does something no other clip does — a tool-brand card (CapCut, tripled) *before* the TikTok bumper, a two-stage close. **The TikTok bumper is almost certainly a shared export-tool artifact, not a deliberate editorial choice — don't treat it as "the correct ending" just because it's the majority. Match the ending to what the brief actually needs**: fade-and-hold when the CTA line should linger, a static brand card when the point is the product, the bumper template when the platform is the point.

**Typographic register may or may not shift mid-video.** Clips 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 hold one caption system for the whole runtime. Clips 7, 8, 10 deliberately switch registers to mark a structural change — bold hook type gives way to smaller "vlog" captions once the pitch turns conversational (7); plain sans gives way to italic serif specifically for inserted testimonial footage from other people (8); bold sans for hooks/interstitials gives way to serif for tutorial narration (10). **Both are legitimate. A register switch should mark an actual structural change (hook→body, host→testimonial), not happen for no reason** — and a single consistent register for the whole piece is just as valid a choice as switching.

**Not every video needs a deep tutorial.** Clip 1 barely shows UI (a couple of App Store frames); clips 6, 9, 10 spend 10+ seconds in dense, multi-stage, callout-annotated screen-recording. The depth of the how-to section scales with the video's actual purpose — a testimonial-style piece doesn't need to justify itself with a feature tour, and a tutorial piece shouldn't rush past the UI to get back to a face.

**Structure can be one continuous host or several stitched-together people.** Most clips are one person for the whole runtime, occasionally cutting to their own B-roll. Clip 8 deliberately cuts to two entirely different speakers mid-video as testimonial/social proof, then returns to the original host for the CTA. This is valid — but when it happens, the *caption* is what has to stay continuous as one throughline; the shot is free to jump between speakers and locations underneath it.

**Deliberate stillness is a tool, not a mandate.** Clips 1, 2, and 6 each hold at least one moment (a static app screenshot, real trade-show footage with no captions at all, a caption-free B-roll run) specifically to let something breathe. Clips 3 and 5 almost never stop moving — everything is layered, multiplying, or transitioning at all times. **Neither is wrong on its own, but if literally everything in an edit is animating with zero held beats, that's a signal to check it against the reference set — most of these clips choose at least one moment to leave alone.**

**Novelty hook devices are per-creator, not universal.** The editable-caption-drag-box gag (clip 5), the ticking counter badge (clip 3), the rotating halo-ring around a word reused later as a testimonial title card (clip 8), two physical framed prints as a before/after (clip 7) — these are each one clip's invention, not a shared grammar. Don't assume any single one of these is expected; they're evidence of the *kind* of inventive device that fits this bar, not a checklist to replicate verbatim.

## The actual checklist, mid-edit

1. **Does this caption land on the exact word/frame it represents?** If not, fix that before anything else — it's the single highest-weighted thing across all ten references.
2. **Is there a visible difference between this emphasis word and the connective words around it**, and is that difference consistent with whatever scheme I've already established in this piece — not borrowed wholesale from one reference clip?
3. **Does the cut/transition line up with caption completion**, or is it arbitrary?
4. **If I'm showing software: is this a real recording with a real cursor, and is there a callout on the specific control being named right now?**
5. **Does the number/brand/claim on screen carry more visual weight than the sentence around it?**
6. **Did the hook start building toward something in the first three seconds**, rather than opening flat?
7. **Have I left anything alone at all** — one static beat, one caption-free run — or is every single second of this piece animating? If it's all motion, check whether that's actually earned or just reflexive.
8. **Is the ending matched to the brief**, not defaulted to whichever template I've seen most often?
9. **If cutting between people or locations, does the caption still read as one unbroken sentence/idea** even while the picture jumps?

That's the bar. Where the ten disagree, the disagreement itself is the information — it means the choice is a legitimate editorial decision to make per-project, not a gap to fill by picking whichever clip I remember best.

**Clip 1 — f0476f42 (43.2s)**

**Cold open (0.00–0.5s):** A single diagonal white brush-stroke/streak sits alone on a blank white field for a full half-second beat before any text appears — a pure graphic flourish, no face, no context. It reads as a transition wipe left mid-motion, used here as a hook-frame rather than a transition. This is the only "dead" white-canvas beat in the clip; everything after it is layered dense.

**Hook block (0.5–3.0s):** A scaled/rotated crop of a kid at a gaming PC (face pixelated/blurred — privacy redaction baked into the source, not a stylistic choice) is composited at an angle on the white background, photo-collage style, with a drop shadow, like a Polaroid tossed on a desk. Text builds word-by-word and holds cumulatively: "this kid" (0.5s) → "makes" added (1.0s) → "$2,000,0" ticking in like an odometer (1.5s) → full "$2,000,000" in bold yellow condensed type, motion-blurred as if slamming into place, with "a month" in a smaller grey sans serif tucked underneath (2.0–2.5s). The dollar figure is the only colored (yellow) text in the whole opening — everything else is black or white. At 2.5s the frame itself starts rotating/zooming as if photo is being flung off-screen, motion-blurred, and by 3.0s a second Polaroid-style photo (different kid, graduation-cap composite, unblurred, smiling) swings in from off-frame with "but hasn't even" stacked in the corner. **Icon/logo interstitial (3.0–3.5s):** The AI-chip icon sits alone against a soft gradient wash background (peach/lavender), then the same icon reappears smaller beside the TikTok logo at 3.5s as the shot cuts back to the host — establishing the icon as "the tool" being introduced before it's named.

Captions "AND UPLOAD" (5.0s) → "YOUR VIDEO" (5.5s) sit centered over the screen-record.
